| [LIT-008](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-008.md) v2 | Modeling and solving an integrated periodic vehicle routing and capacitated facility location problem in the context of solid waste collection | González et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2504.10648](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10648). The paper couples bin-capacity choice with weekly periodic capacitated routing (Sunday off, cyclic). Service time depends on the chosen bin combination, which gives an MIQP; a Glover linearisation turns it into a MILP. It solves both with Gurobi 10 for 8 h, and also with a binary-mask + permutation GA (CX 0.8, EM 0.05, pop 100, 10,000 generations). On five 12-point instances Gurobi stops at 26–32% optimality gaps. The best-of-30 GA overall cost is on average −0.08% vs the MILP incumbent and +1.70% vs the MIQP incumbent; the GA mean or median is +3.75% and +5.61%. The GA routes better (−5.75% and −5.74% routing cost) but buys much more bin capacity (+19.88% and +22.59%). On 40–163-point Bahía Blanca instances the GA returns feasible solutions in 0.72–5.58 h per run, with no bound to compare against. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-015); worth reading narrowly, for its formulation (Eqs. 1–2m, with the linearisation in 3a–5) and its public Bahía Blanca instances. | [LIT-050](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-050.md) v2 | Mean-Field-Type Game Theory with Rosenblatt Noise | Tembine et al. (2025), [ARXIV-2506.08025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08025). The paper's control and game results use linear state feedback, and they depend on the Rosenblatt noise only through its covariance, which is exactly fBM's with the same H. They are therefore identical to the fBM results. The ergodic LQ gain (Thm 4), K̂ = −[b₁ + √(b₁² + 4H(1−H)b₂²q/r)]/(2b₂(1−H)), is correct and reduces to the Brownian LQR gain at H = ½. But the paper's headline "suboptimality of noise approximation" (§VI-A, repeated for the variance-aware control, zero-sum, non-zero-sum and MFTG settings) holds only against surrogates with a different covariance; against fBM with the same H it is false. The ML claim that Rosenblatt "super-diffusion transformers" "significantly enhance the performance of generative machine intelligence models" (§XIV-C) has no model, training, dataset or experiment behind it anywhere in the paper. | Rejected — read in full 2026-09-25 (NOTE-068); not worth a reader's time. The control-theoretic results are earlier papers' (its refs [43]–[46]) restated. Its central new claim, that Gaussian and fBM surrogates give suboptimal control, is false for fBM with matching H, since the costs depend only on covariance. Its empirical sections are unsourced vignettes: numbers without references, "Rosenblatt shape" fits without any fitting procedure, and data from the first author's own startups. Its ML claim is an assertion with no model or experiment. A reader wanting Rosenblatt-noise LQ control should go to Čoupek–Duncan–Maslowski–Pasik-Duncan (CDC 2018, ref [43]) and Čoupek–Duncan–Pasik-Duncan (SPA 2022, ref [27]). |

| [LIT-352](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-352.md) v2 | A numerical algorithm for block-diagonal decomposition of matrix *-algebras with application to semidefinite programming | Murota et al. The structure theorem it relies on, Theorem 3.1(C) "if 𝒯 is irreducible then 𝒯 = Mₙ", is false over ℝ as stated. | [LIT-868](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-868.md) | A Generalized Information-Theoretic Framework for the Emergence of Hierarchical Abstractions in Resource-Limited Systems | Larsson, Maity and Tsiotras (2022), Entropy 24(6):809. Treats a pruning of a fixed quadtree as a deterministic encoder of the grid and maximises Σβ_i I(T;Y_i) − Σγ_j I(T;Z_j) − αI(T;X) over such prunings. Every term splits over interior nodes (p(t)·JS of the children's conditionals; p(t)H of the split), so a bottom-up recursion (G-tree search) returns the optimal tree with fewest leaves in linear time. Recovers the IB and IB-with-side-information trees as special cases and proves the latter is always a pruning of the former. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-676](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-676.md)); worth reading as an exact solution of a structured information-bottleneck problem: when the encoder must be a pruning of a fixed tree (here the dyadic quadtree of a grid), every information term splits over the interior nodes, a node's share of I(T;Y) being p(t) times the Jensen–Shannon divergence of its children's p(y\|·) and its share of I(T;X) being p(t)H(Π). A bottom-up recursion, G(t) = max{ΔJ(t) + Σ G(children), 0}, then returns the optimal tree with the fewest leaves for any weighted sum of relevance, irrelevance and compression terms, in time linear in the grid. A greedy top-down search can miss all the relevant information, because a node whose children predict Y alike gains nothing however much its grandchildren differ. Adding an irrelevance penalty can only prune the plain IB tree. The hierarchy is given, not found: what "emerges" is which coarse-graining of a fixed quadtree to keep. |

| [LIT-1083](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1083.md) | An Efficient, Cost-Driven Index Selection Tool for Microsoft SQL Server | Chaudhuri and Narasayya (1997), VLDB '97. The AutoAdmin tool picks at most k indexes (single- or two-column, clustered or not) for a given workload of SQL statements, minimising the unweighted sum of the optimizer's estimated costs of those statements, with hypothetical ("what-if") indexes made visible to the optimizer by loading their statistics into the catalog. Its contribution is search efficiency: candidates are restricted to indexes in some single query's best configuration, enumeration is Greedy(m, k) (an exhaustive seed of m indexes, then greedy additions), costs of most configurations are derived from a few "atomic" ones, and two-column indexes are generated only from winning single columns. On five TPC-D workloads this cut running time to 10–24% of a baseline, with estimated-cost quality 0–7% worse, and Greedy(2, 4) matched the exhaustive optimum on four of five workloads and was within 1% on the fifth. The cost model has no build cost, no storage term and no frequency weights, the budget is a count of indexes, the workload is fixed, there is no guarantee for the greedy step, and quality is never measured by executing anything. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the VLDB Endowment's proceedings PDF (www.vldb.org/conf/1997/P146.PDF, pp. 146–155, a scan with an OCR layer; tables and figures read from page images), which refuses plain requests from this environment (HTTP 403) and was served when the request carried a browser User-Agent. Worth reading as the founding paper of optimizer-driven ("what-if") index selection in practice: at most k indexes chosen for a fixed workload of SQL statements to minimise the unweighted sum of the optimizer's estimated costs, made affordable by per-query candidate selection, Greedy(m, k) enumeration with an exhaustive seed, derived costs from atomic configurations, and two-column indexes grown from single-column winners (4–10 times faster than a baseline, 0–7% worse by estimated cost, on five TPC-D workloads). For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it prices organizing ahead no differently from Finkelstein et al. ([LIT-1084](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1084.md)), and in fewer terms: upkeep through the workload's update statements, but no build cost, no storage term, no frequency weights and no changing workload, so "paid once" and staleness stay unpriced; what it adds is that deciding the arrangement has its own cost, and evidence (not a bound) that greedy choice works when index interactions are few and local. | [LIT-1084](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1084.md) | Physical database design for relational databases | Finkelstein, Schkolnick and Tiberio (1988), ACM TODS 13(1). DBDSGN chooses, for each table, one clustered (ordering) index and a set of nonclustered indices to minimise a frequency-weighted sum of per-statement costs (access, tuple update, index maintenance) plus a weighted storage term, under an optional page limit, taking every cost from the System R optimizer's own estimates rather than an external model. Statement costs for any configuration are computed exactly from "atomic" configurations with at most one index per table (Propositions 1 and 2), so the optimizer is consulted a linear rather than exponential number of times per table; with no elimination heuristics and a full search the tool finds the optimum, but only with respect to the optimizer's estimates. The paper gives one worked example and no measurement of actual execution, and its claims that the heuristics usually find the best solutions are not backed by reported data. | [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md) | Selection of views to materialize in a data warehouse | Gupta (1997), ICDT '97. Gupta states view selection on general AND-OR view graphs as minimizing frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget. He proves greedy guarantees of 1 − 1/e (about 63%) of the optimal benefit, with the budget overrun by one view or up to double, but almost all of them assume no updates. Maintenance cost enters exactly one theorem: AND view graphs (each view has one way of being computed) in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. For OR view graphs, which include Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman's data cube, the paper sets update costs aside outright, so it does not add upkeep to that problem. Maintenance is an abstract per-update charge for keeping a view consistent. Nothing prices building a view, tolerated staleness or deferred refresh, and there are no experiments. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the author's PostScript copy on the Stanford InfoLab papers server (infolab.stanford.edu/pub/papers/SelectionViews.ps, 15 pp., dated March 1997, linked from the warehousing project's publication page; Unpaywall and OpenAlex report the DOI closed). Worth reading as the general statement of view selection: AND-OR view graphs with query and update frequencies, and an objective of frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget, with greedy guarantees of 1 − 1/e of the optimal benefit when space may overrun. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it gives the joint objective in form: reuse against per-update upkeep under capacity. It charges no build cost, leaves the maintenance cost abstract, and models only keeping views consistent, not tolerating or acting on stale ones. Its guarantees with maintenance cost hold only for AND view graphs in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. For the data cube of [LIT-1094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1094.md) it assumes no updates, so it does not add upkeep to that problem. That came in Gupta and Mumick's maintenance-time-constrained follow-up (ICDT 1999), read afterwards as LIT-1092. |
| [LIT-1092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1092.md) | Selection of Views to Materialize Under a Maintenance Cost Constraint | Gupta and Mumick (1999), ICDT '99. Gupta and Mumick choose views to materialize so as to minimize frequency-weighted query cost subject to a cap S on total maintenance time, the sum over chosen views of update frequency times a per-update maintenance cost that depends on which other views are stored. Because storing one view can make another cheaper to maintain, benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and the single-view greedy of earlier work can be arbitrarily bad. For OR view graphs (each view computed from one other, as in data cubes) a greedy that adds whole "inverted tree sets" gets at least 1 − 1/e (63%) of the benefit of an optimal solution that may use as much maintenance as the greedy did, the greedy using up to 2S, assuming no inverted-tree piece of the optimum alone exceeds S (Theorem 1, unproved here); without that assumption it gets half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance (Theorem 2). Each greedy stage enumerates exponentially many sets in general; for general AND-OR graphs there is only an exact A* search with exponential worst case. Upkeep is a budget, not a term traded against query savings; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled, and the experiments are on random graphs of 10 to 25 nodes. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' PostScript copy on Stanford InfoLab's papers server (infolab.stanford.edu/pub/papers/update.ps, 18 pages, dated 8 October 1998, the ICDT '99 camera-ready, not the 2005 TKDE journal version; not compared with Springer's typeset pages). Worth reading as the first view-selection result that budgets maintenance time instead of space, and for its demonstration that upkeep is not additive: storing one view can make others cheaper to maintain, so benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and single-view greedy can be arbitrarily bad. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it shows upkeep priced as a budget, U(M) = Σ update frequency × per-update maintenance cost given the other stored views, with query cost the only objective; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled (every view is refreshed in a nightly batch). Its guarantee answers the open problem of [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md) only for OR view graphs: 1 − 1/e of an optimum's benefit while using up to twice the budget, under an assumption on the optimum, or half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance without it, with the theorems stated but not proved and a greedy whose stages are exponential in general (including on data cubes). General AND-OR graphs get only an exact A* search. It does not close the question, and comes no closer to a joint cost model than [LIT-1095](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1095.md). |
| [LIT-1094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1094.md) | Implementing data cubes efficiently | Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman (1996), SIGMOD '96. Treats a data cube's group-by queries as a lattice in which a query can be answered from any stored ancestor, prices a query at the number of rows of the smallest materialized ancestor, and chooses which views to precompute. Choosing k views to maximize the total reduction in query cost (the "benefit") is NP-complete; a greedy rule that adds the view of largest marginal benefit gets at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimal benefit, a bound that is tight, holds unchanged with query-frequency weights, and weakens to 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view takes more than a fraction f of it. The cost of building views is represented only by their size, maintenance and updates are not modelled, the data are static, and the bound is on benefit, not on query cost. On TPC-D data the greedy order reaches nearly the minimum total query time with five views and barely more space than the base view. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' 25-page version on Stanford InfoLab's papers server (infolab.stanford.edu/pub/papers/cube.ps, TeX run of 8 January 1996), not the SIGMOD typesetting, which the ACM Digital Library refused (403); the two were not compared. Worth reading as the standard source on choosing which precomputed answers to store when each query is answered from its cheapest stored ancestor: the lattice of group-by views, the linear cost model (rows of the ancestor scanned), NP-completeness, and a greedy rule whose total benefit, the saving against storing the base view alone, is at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimum for a budget of k views, tight, unchanged with fixed query frequencies, and only 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view exceeds a fraction f of it. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) and [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows the precomputed-answer term the four earlier readings lacked, with a stored answer's value counted over every query it serves and marginal on what is already stored (sharpening [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md)'s break-even); it does not price build cost (space is a proxy), upkeep or staleness (the data are static and derived answers exact), timing or deadlines, uncertain workloads, or the medium of retrieval, so it is a model of the speed bugs only in naming the category, an analogy with one usable term for filed arguments, silent on the bias of reused inferences, and not about LEGO bins. |

| [LIT-1105](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1105.md) | Balancing Performance and Data Freshness in Web Database Servers | Labrinidis and Roussopoulos (2003), VLDB 2003. The paper poses Online View Selection for a web server whose database takes updates while serving requests: choose, as the workload runs, which page fragments (WebViews) to keep stored and refreshed on every update and which to cache and invalidate, so as to minimize mean response time while the fraction of fresh fragments served (QoD) stays above a threshold θ. Its algorithm, OVIS(θ), estimates per fragment the response-time and QoD change of switching, and periodically switches up to MAX_CHANGE fragments greedily, spending a QoD surplus on speed or buying back a deficit; it materializes everything when it detects backlog. Nothing is proved: optimality of the greedy step is asserted, and the evidence is one synthetic simulation with fixed costs, in which OVIS kept QoD near θ, answered faster than caching alone, and recovered from overload. Upkeep and query savings share one cost, but staleness is a constraint set by the user, not a priced term, and build cost, switching cost and storage are absent. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 ([NOTE-911](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-911.md)) from the VLDB Endowment's copy of the 2003 conference paper (www.vldb.org/conf/2003/papers/S13P01.pdf, 12 pp.; Crossref pages 393–404), whose bitmap fonts made OCR necessary; the 2004 VLDB Journal version was not read. Worth reading as the first online view-selection algorithm that trades response time against a measured freshness: OVIS(θ) periodically moves up to a fixed number of page fragments between cached-and-invalidated and stored-and-refreshed, greedily, to keep the share of fresh fragments served above θ at the least response time, and materializes everything when it detects backlog. | [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md) | Adaptive Precision Setting for Cached Approximate Values | Olston et al. (2001), SIGMOD 2001. Olston, Loo and Widom set the width of each cached interval adaptively to minimize total refresh traffic. A narrow interval is escaped often (value-initiated refreshes, cost C_vr); a wide one is too imprecise for queries more often (query-initiated refreshes, cost C_qr). Under a model in which these probabilities go as 1/W² and W, the expected cost rate is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr, ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, and a rule that widens on value-initiated and narrows on query-initiated refreshes, with probabilities set by ρ, reached within 1% to 5% of the best fixed width in simulation. That the rule converges is argued, not proved. With exact copies required it matched an adaptive exact-caching algorithm, and where imprecision was allowed it beat it. Staleness is priced as refresh traffic only: there is no build cost, no cost of a wrong answer, and the interval is never wrong. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the copy in the University of Pennsylvania's repository (ScholarlyCommons cis_papers 1351, repository.upenn.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/92340f91-673c-435e-9b4e-b24072d4d96b/content), the camera-ready text with printed pages 355–366. Worth reading as the one model the record holds in which staleness and upkeep are traded in a single objective: a cached interval of width W is escaped (a pushed refresh, cost C_vr) more often when narrow and is too loose for queries (an exact fetch, cost C_qr) more often when wide, and under the paper's model the least expected cost is where ρ·P_vr = P_qr with ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr ([THEORY-386](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-386.md)); a rule that widens on one kind of refresh and narrows on the other came within 1–5% of the best fixed width in simulation and, restricted to exact copies, matched an adaptive cache-or-not algorithm ([THEORY-377](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-377.md)). For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it prices staleness as refresh traffic, with no build cost, no stored answers and no cost of a wrong answer, since the source guarantees validity. For [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it gives upkeep and per-use verification a common dial, but only where a source sees every change; for [CLAIM-308](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-308.md) its exact-caching case is a forecast-free counting rule justified in expectation, not in the worst case, and once staleness is admitted the two-state choice becomes a continuum with an interior optimum. |
| [LIT-1117](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1117.md) | Offering a Precision-Performance Tradeoff for Aggregation Queries over Replicated Data | Olston and Widom (2000), VLDB 2000. Olston and Widom propose TRAPP: caches hold, for each numeric value, an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, the source pushing a refresh whenever the value leaves it. A query carries a precision constraint R, and the system chooses which values to fetch exactly so that the answer interval is at most R wide whatever the true values, at least total refresh cost. For SUM (and AVG without a predicate) that choice is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and polynomial with equal costs; COUNT and MIN have simple rules. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and the cost of the source-side upkeep that guarantees this, and of setting the bound widths, is outside the optimization. The one experiment is 90 stock prices with random costs. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the VLDB Endowment's open copy of the proceedings paper (www.vldb.org/conf/2000/P144.pdf, pp. 144–155; the server needs a browser User-Agent). Worth reading as the source of the idea that a cached value can be held as an interval its source guarantees, so that staleness becomes a bounded, stated imprecision instead of an unknown error, and a query buys precision down by paying for exact reads; for SUM, choosing the cheapest reads that meet a width R is a 0/1 knapsack problem ([THEORY-364](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-364.md)). For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it gives staleness a unit (bound width against a query's tolerance) and prices only the query side: the source's upkeep that makes the bound a guarantee, and the choice of bound widths, are assumed and uncosted, imprecision is a hard constraint rather than a loss, and a stale read can never be wrong. For [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it sharpens "verification" into a per-use decision against a stated tolerance, but rests on a source that watches every copy, which a filed argument lacks, so it does not price the cost of reusing an obsolete conclusion; it does not bear on [CLAIM-308](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-308.md)'s rent-or-buy argument. [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md) prices the upkeep side. |
| [LIT-1118](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1118.md) | WebView Materialization | Labrinidis and Roussopoulos (2000), SIGMOD 2000. For a page built from database queries, the paper compares three ways to serve it on a server with online updates: compute it on each request (virt), store the query result in the DBMS and refresh it on every update (matdb), or store the finished page as a file at the web server and rewrite it on every update (matweb). It gives a cost model summing access and update costs by their frequencies and states the selection problem (choose a policy per page to minimize mean response time, no space limit, no staleness allowed), but gives no algorithm for it. On one Apache/Informix testbed with cheap indexed queries, matweb answered 10 to 230 times faster than the other two at all loads tried, and matdb was slower than virt whenever there were updates, because reading the stored result cost about as much as recomputing it. Staleness is defined as the delay from update to reply, sketched, and never measured; build cost and storage are outside the model. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 ([NOTE-908](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-908.md)) from the authors' camera-ready copy on the University of Maryland Opsis project page (www.cs.umd.edu/projects/opsis/papers/2000/webviews.pdf, 12 pp., dated 1 March 2000); the ACM Digital Library copy returned 403. Worth reading as the first cost model for choosing, per database-generated web page, between computing it on request, storing the query result in the DBMS, and storing the finished page at the web server, with every stored copy refreshed on each update; on one Apache/Informix testbed the page stored at the web server answered 10 to 230 times faster, and the result stored in the DBMS lost to recomputation whenever there were updates, because reading it cost about as much as rebuilding it. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it prices access and upkeep by frequency and adds where the copy is stored, but forbids staleness, has no build cost or storage term, and states the selection problem without an algorithm; for [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it shows filing failing through access cost alone, and upkeep slowing the unfiled reads that share its resource (by 236% in its model check). |
| [LIT-1119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1119.md) | Synchronizing a Database to Improve Freshness | Cho and Garcia-Molina (2000), SIGMOD 2000. For a local copy of N items, each changing as an independent Poisson process with a known rate and refreshed at fixed intervals under a fixed total refresh rate, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy fresher and younger on average than refreshing in proportion to change rate, under any distribution of rates (proved in the technical report by convexity). The freshness-optimal allocation is neither: it rises and then falls with change rate, and gives no refresh at all to items that change too fast for the budget, while the age-optimal allocation rises slowly with change rate. On estimates from 270 web sites, proportional, uniform and optimal refresh give freshness 0.12, 0.57 and 0.62. Every item matters equally, staleness is a time average with no access or query model, the refresh budget is fixed rather than priced, and refresh, change and its detection are free of any other cost. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the conference version as published, the PDF of SIGMOD 2000 pp. 117–128 served by ACM SIGMOD's SIGMOD Record site for the June 2000 proceedings issue (sigmodrecord.org/publications/sigmodRecord/0006/pdfs/Synchronizing%20a%20Database%20to%20Improve%20Freshness.pdf), with the proofs it defers checked in the authors' 1999 Stanford technical report as hosted on a KTH course page. Worth reading as the standard definition of a copy's freshness and age under Poisson change, and for the result that, under a fixed refresh budget, refreshing every item equally beats refreshing in proportion to change rate for any distribution of rates, while the freshness-optimal allocation gives nothing to items that change too fast to follow. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it is the first reading that prices staleness instead of forbidding it, but as an objective under a fixed budget, with no reads, no query savings and no build cost, so it supplies the staleness term and not the joint model; for [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it models the re-checking term per unit time and by rate of change, not per use, and does not price the cost of a stale use. |
| [LIT-1155](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1155.md) v2 | The geometry of graphs and some of its algorithmic applications | Linial, London & Rabinovich (1995), *Combinatorica* 15(2): 215–245. Every n-point metric embeds in O(log n)-dimensional Euclidean space with distortion O(log n) (Bourgain's theorem as Theorem 3.2(1) states it). The paper reproves the distortion by a randomized map to distances from O(log² n) random sets, takes the dimension from Johnson–Lindenstrauss, and computes the least Euclidean distortion of any finite metric by semidefinite programming. Constant-degree expanders need distortion Ω(log n) in ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension (Proposition 4.2), so the bound is tight. The max-flow/min-cut gap for k commodities is O(log k), with a deterministic algorithm (Theorem 4.1). | Active — read 2026-10-16 ([NOTE-928](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-928.md)) in full; worth reading as the place where Bourgain's O(log n) embedding of finite metrics into Euclidean space is restated, reproved by distances to random sets of every scale, and shown tight: constant-degree expanders need distortion Ω(log n) in ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension, because their gap between multicommodity flow and cut is Ω(log n). The same embeddings bound that gap by O(log k) for k commodities. Read it knowing that the O(log n) dimension comes from Johnson–Lindenstrauss, not from the construction, which uses O(log² n) coordinates; that the lower bound rests on Leighton and Rao's gap, cited; that constants are unspecified; and that it says nothing about trees in ℓ₂, for which Sala et al. cite it. Filed as [THEORY-394](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-394.md). |
| [LIT-1212](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1212.md) | Multiple-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) for multiobjective optimization | Désidéri (2012; first as an INRIA report, 2009). When a design point is not Pareto-optimal, a descent direction common to all smooth criteria exists and can be constructed (the minimum-norm element of the convex hull of the gradients); steepest descent along it converges to a Pareto-stationary point. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-18, not read. Registered from the exchange of 2026-10-17, "Synthesis opportunities analysis" (workbench entries of 2026-10-18). No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-1217](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1217.md) | Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance | Castro & Liskov (1999). A replication algorithm that tolerates Byzantine faults in asynchronous networks such as the Internet and is fast enough to use: a Byzantine-fault-tolerant NFS built on it was only 3% slower than unreplicated NFS. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-18, not read. Registered from the exchange of 2026-10-17, "Synthesis opportunities analysis" (workbench entries of 2026-10-18). No NOTE is filed. |
